interview.question: What does SetStateAction<S> represent?
interview.answer: SetStateAction<S> is a union of S and an updater function `(prevState: S) => S`. This allows a setter to receive either the next value directly or a calculation based on the previous state.
interview.followUp: Why use the updater form for multiple dependent updates? React queues updater functions and applies them to the previous state during the next render, so each update can build on the preceding one.

interview.question: How does React process the function form?
interview.answer: The updater function should be pure, accept the pending state, and return the next state. React queues it and evaluates it during the next render.
interview.followUp: What should an updater avoid? It should not perform side effects or mutate the pending state; compute and return the next state instead.

interview.question: How do the two union branches differ?
interview.answer: A direct value replaces the state with that value, while an updater function derives a replacement value from the previous state. The generic S is the state type in both branches.
interview.followUp: How can a component update object state safely? Return a new object, commonly by copying the previous object and changing only the intended property.

keyPoints: The setter accepts either a state value or a function that computes the next state.
Updater functions must be pure and return the next state rather than causing side effects.
React queues updater functions and uses them to determine the state for a later render.
Queued updater functions are applied during the next render in order.
gotchas: Reading the state variable immediately after calling its setter still gives the value from the current render.

startTransition.summary: startTransition marks synchronous state updates as non-urgent Transitions. React can render the affected UI in the background while keeping urgent interactions responsive.
startTransition.explanation: Call startTransition with a synchronous action that performs state updates. React invokes the action immediately and treats state updates scheduled during that call as non-urgent Transitions, allowing background rendering; use useTransition instead when pending status must be displayed.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: A synchronous function that updates state by calling one or more setter functions. React invokes it immediately without arguments and marks synchronous updates during its execution as Transitions.

example.title: Marking a tab update as a Transition
example.explanation: Wraps a non-urgent tab-selection update so React can render it in the background without blocking more urgent interactions.

useCases.title: Keep navigation responsive
useCases.scenario: A component changes tabs or navigates between views and the next view may require substantial rendering.

useCases.title: Start a Transition outside Hooks
useCases.scenario: A library or event handler outside a component needs to classify a state update as non-urgent.

useCases.title: Preserve the current UI
useCases.scenario: A state update should avoid replacing the current UI with an unnecessary loading indicator during background rendering.

interview.question: What does startTransition do?
interview.answer: startTransition marks state updates performed by its synchronous callback as Transitions. React treats those updates as non-urgent and can render them in the background.
interview.followUp: How do you show progress for the transition? Use useTransition, whose returned startTransition is paired with an isPending flag.

interview.question: Is the callback deferred?
interview.answer: The action is called immediately with no arguments. State updates scheduled synchronously while it runs receive Transition priority.
interview.followUp: Would setTimeout inside the callback automatically remain part of the Transition? No; delayed updates occur outside the synchronous callback and must be wrapped separately.

interview.question: When should you use startTransition instead of useTransition?
interview.answer: startTransition returns nothing and does not expose pending state. It is useful outside components or Hooks, such as in a data library.
interview.followUp: Which API is preferable inside a component when pending UI is needed? useTransition, because it supplies isPending and a transition function.

keyPoints: Use it for state changes whose rendering can happen without blocking urgent user interactions.
Wrapping a setter call changes how React schedules that update rather than changing the state value itself.
The normal pattern is to place one or more state setter calls inside the function passed to startTransition.
gotchas: Use useTransition when the UI needs an isPending value or another pending indicator.
The callback is not deferred like setTimeout; do not expect startTransition to postpone executing the action.
Only updates made synchronously inside the callback are marked; updates after asynchronous work need another transition wrapper.

StrictMode.sourceTitle: Fixing bugs found by re-running Effects in development
StrictMode.summary: StrictMode enables extra development-only checks for a component subtree. It helps reveal impure rendering, missing Effect or ref cleanup, and deprecated API usage early.
StrictMode.explanation: StrictMode is a development-only wrapper that activates extra checks for the component tree inside it. React uses those checks to expose impure rendering, missing Effect or ref cleanup, and deprecated API usage before these problems reach production.
StrictMode.returns: A component wrapper that renders its children and enables additional development-only checks for the enclosed tree.

example.title: Enable Strict Mode for an application
example.explanation: Wrap the application root to enable Strict Mode checks throughout the rendered component tree during development.

useCases.title: Application-wide bug detection
useCases.scenario: Enable diagnostics across an entire application during development.

useCases.title: Scoped diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Inspect a feature or subtree without changing the rest of the application.

useCases.title: Cleanup verification
useCases.scenario: Detect missing Effect and ref cleanup before production.

keyPoints: Use StrictMode as a development diagnostic wrapper for catching common component bugs earlier.
The wrapper applies its additional checks to the component tree placed inside it.
React performs an additional render in development to reveal render logic that is not pure.
Effects receive an extra development-only setup cycle so missing cleanup becomes visible.
Ref callback cleanup problems are exposed by an additional development-only ref-callback cycle.
Strict Mode checks the wrapped components for deprecated API usage.
Wrap the root element with StrictMode to enable checks across the whole application.
gotchas: The extra renders, Effect runs, ref-callback runs, and deprecation checks occur only during development; they do not represent production behavior.

Suspense.summary: Suspense displays a fallback while descendant UI is not ready, then reveals that UI when it can render. Use boundaries to define loading regions and coordinate progressive or streamed content.
Suspense.explanation: Suspense creates a boundary around child UI that may not be ready during rendering. When a child suspends, React temporarily renders the fallback; once the child is ready, React replaces the fallback with the child content. Boundaries can also coordinate progressive loading and server-rendered streaming.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: The React nodes to render when ready. If they suspend during rendering, the boundary renders fallback instead.

parameters.name: fallback
parameters.description: The alternate React node shown while children have not finished loading.

Suspense.returns: A React element that renders children when ready and fallback while children are suspended.

example.title: Lazy component with a loading boundary
example.explanation: A lazy component suspends while its module loads, so the boundary displays a lightweight fallback and then renders the loaded component.

useCases.title: Code splitting with lazy
useCases.scenario: A component's JavaScript module is loaded on demand and may suspend on first render.

useCases.title: Progressive loading with nested boundaries
useCases.scenario: Different parts of a page become ready at different times and should reveal in coordinated groups.

useCases.title: Streaming server rendering
useCases.scenario: Server-rendered content can be sent in independently renderable regions.

interview.question: What problem does Suspense solve, and when does it show the fallback?
interview.answer: Suspense renders its fallback when a descendant suspends while rendering, then switches back to the children when they are ready. A suspended boundary can wait for lazy component code, a Promise read with use, or certain stylesheet loads.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid hiding content that is already visible during navigation? Wrap the non-urgent update in startTransition so React can delay the fallback replacement.

interview.question: What makes a good Suspense fallback?
interview.answer: The fallback is an alternate React node rendered in place of unfinished children. It should usually be lightweight, such as a spinner or skeleton, and it must not itself suspend unless an enclosing boundary can handle that suspension.
interview.followUp: What happens if the fallback suspends? React activates the closest parent Suspense boundary.

interview.question: How can Suspense coordinate progressive loading and server rendering?
interview.answer: Suspense boundaries let an application choose which regions reveal together and which progressively reveal through nested loading states. During server rendering, React includes the fallback in the HTML and later replaces it in the browser with the saved content.
interview.followUp: How can a server-rendered page reveal independent regions sooner? Place separate Suspense boundaries around regions that can load independently, allowing their content to stream separately.

keyPoints: Wrap potentially delayed UI in a Suspense boundary to provide declarative loading behavior.
The children prop contains the UI that the boundary protects.
The fallback prop supplies the temporary UI shown while the protected content is unavailable.
React changes between fallback and children automatically as the boundary's readiness changes.
Code loaded through React.lazy can suspend, making Suspense the place to present its loading state.
Promise-based rendering with use can keep a boundary from revealing content until the value is available.
Suspense boundaries can be positioned around any application subtree to establish a loading region.
gotchas: A fallback can itself suspend; React then uses the nearest enclosing Suspense boundary.
An already visible boundary may switch to its fallback during an update; use startTransition for non-urgent updates to avoid that undesirable replacement.
Suspended content is revealed with batching behavior, so multiple boundaries that become ready within the interval may appear together.

SyntheticEvent.summary: React.SyntheticEvent is the general TypeScript type for React event objects. It follows the DOM Event model while smoothing over browser inconsistencies and exposing the original event through nativeEvent.
SyntheticEvent.explanation: React.SyntheticEvent is the TypeScript base type for React event objects. React event objects follow the standard DOM Event shape while smoothing over browser differences, and they expose the original browser event through nativeEvent.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: The React event object delivered to an event handler; generic parameters can describe the native event and current target element.

example.title: Reading a React event object
example.explanation: The handler receives React’s event object, uses a standard event method, and reads the element associated with the handler.

useCases.title: Generic event-handler typing
useCases.scenario: Type a handler when no narrower React event type covers the DOM event you receive.

useCases.title: Event control and inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect or cancel an interaction using standard event properties and methods.

useCases.title: Native event access
useCases.scenario: Reach browser-specific details that are available only on the underlying DOM event.

interview.question: What is React.SyntheticEvent?
interview.answer: SyntheticEvent is the base TypeScript type for React events. React event objects provide standard Event properties and methods while addressing browser inconsistencies.
interview.followUp: How do you access the browser event? Read the React event’s nativeEvent property, while remembering that its native type may differ from the React event name.

interview.question: Which common operations and properties does a React event object provide?
interview.answer: Use preventDefault() to stop the browser’s default action, and stopPropagation() to stop propagation through the React tree. Properties such as defaultPrevented and currentTarget let the handler inspect event state and attachment.
interview.followUp: How can you determine whether cancellation already occurred? Check isDefaultPrevented() or the defaultPrevented property.

interview.question: How would you type a generic React event handler in TypeScript?
interview.answer: Type the handler parameter as React.SyntheticEvent with an appropriate element type when a more specific event type is not available. For example, React.SyntheticEvent<HTMLButtonElement> describes an event handled by a button.
interview.followUp: When the event is one of React’s specifically documented event types, prefer that narrower type so event-specific fields are available.

keyPoints: The React event interface resembles the browser Event interface while normalizing browser behavior.
currentTarget identifies the element where the active React handler is attached.
target can be a descendant that originated the event rather than the element running the handler.
nativeEvent exposes the underlying DOM Event when direct browser-level access is needed.
stopPropagation() prevents the event from continuing through React’s event tree.
gotchas: Do not assume every React event corresponds one-to-one with a native browser event.
Use nativeEvent when browser-specific access to the original DOM event is required.

use.summary: React's use API reads a Promise or context during rendering. Promise reads suspend while pending, and unlike ordinary Hooks, use can be called in conditions and loops.
use.explanation: Call use(resource) while rendering a component or custom Hook to read a Promise or context. A pending Promise suspends the component until it resolves, while a context produces its current value; unlike ordinary Hooks, use may appear in conditions and loops, but not in try/catch blocks.

parameters.name: resource
parameters.description: The resource whose value should be read; the documented resource types are a Promise or context.

use.returns: The resolved Promise value or the current context value; a pending Promise suspends rendering.

example.title: Reading a Promise with use
example.explanation: Pass a Promise to use; React suspends the component while it is pending and renders the resolved value afterward.

useCases.title: Read asynchronous resources with Suspense
useCases.scenario: A component needs data represented by a Promise and should show fallback UI until it is ready.

useCases.title: Read context conditionally
useCases.scenario: A component only needs a context value in one branch or while iterating over items.

useCases.title: Compose resource reads
useCases.scenario: A custom Hook needs to expose render-time access to a Promise or context.

interview.question: What does React's use API do?
interview.answer: use(resource) reads a Promise or context during rendering. If the Promise is pending, the component suspends; after resolution, rendering can use its value.
interview.followUp: How does use differ from useContext? use can read context conditionally or inside loops, whereas useContext must be called at the component's top level.

interview.question: Can use be called conditionally?
interview.answer: Unlike ordinary Hooks, use may be called inside conditions and loops. It still must be called from a component or Hook, and the Promise itself must be passed to it.
interview.followUp: What restriction remains around exception handling? The call cannot be placed in try/catch/finally, so errors should be handled through React's supported error-handling mechanisms.

interview.question: What happens when use receives a pending Promise?
interview.answer: A component that calls use with a pending Promise suspends while waiting for the Promise. A Suspense boundary can provide the fallback UI during that suspended render.
interview.followUp: What should code avoid when consuming a Promise? It should not read promise.status or promise.value directly; React must receive the Promise through use.

keyPoints: The API reads supported render-time resources, chiefly Promises and context values.
Passing a context returns the value supplied by the nearest matching provider.
Promise reads integrate with Suspense: pending work pauses the component's render.
Its call-site rule is more flexible than ordinary Hooks, allowing branches and iteration.
gotchas: Do not inspect Promise internals to avoid use; pass the Promise to React instead.

use client.summary: The 'use client' directive marks a module and its transitive dependencies as client code in React Server Components. It creates a server-client boundary so interactive components can run in the browser.
use client.explanation: Place the directive at the beginning of a module to establish a server-to-client boundary. The module and its transitive dependencies become client code, enabling browser interactivity such as state and event handlers; values crossing from server-evaluated modules must be components or supported serializable props.

example.title: A client component
example.explanation: This module is compiled as client code, so the component can use state and event handlers.

useCases.title: Enable interactive UI
useCases.scenario: A component needs useState, event handlers, or other browser-side interactivity.

useCases.title: Split server and client rendering
useCases.scenario: A server-rendered tree needs to include a browser-executed subtree.

useCases.title: Define a client dependency subtree
useCases.scenario: A shared module contains dependencies that must be bundled for the browser.

interview.question: What does 'use client' do?
interview.answer: It marks a module as client code for React Server Components. The module’s transitive dependencies are also evaluated on the client, and a compatible bundler treats the import as a server-client boundary.
interview.followUp: Does every component used below a client component need its own directive? No; transitive dependencies are already client code, so another directive is unnecessary.

interview.question: Where must the directive appear, and when is it redundant?
interview.answer: The directive must occur at the very beginning of the file, above imports or other code; comments are allowed before it. It has no effect when the module is imported from another client-rendered module.
interview.followUp: Can a module without the directive still run on the client? Yes. A component can be evaluated on the client when it is a transitive dependency or is imported and used by a Client Component.

interview.question: What can cross from a server module into a client module?
interview.answer: Server-evaluated modules may import values from a client module only when those values are React components or supported serializable prop values intended for a Client Component. This keeps the server-client boundary transferable.
interview.followUp: Why does this restriction matter? The boundary must carry data that the client-side component model and compatible bundler can represent across environments.

keyPoints: The directive identifies a module as client-side code in React Server Components.
Its client classification propagates through the module’s dependency subtree.
A compatible bundler uses the import as the split between server and browser execution.
Components declared in the marked module are treated as Client Components.
Without the directive or a client dependency relationship, component usage is considered server-side.
gotchas: Put the directive before imports and executable code; comments may appear before it.
Adding the directive to an already client-rendered dependency does not create another meaningful boundary.
Do not pass arbitrary non-serializable values from server-evaluated modules across the boundary.

use server.summary: `'use server'` marks an async server-side function as callable from client-side code. Client calls become network requests, with serializable arguments and results handled by the framework.
use server.explanation: `'use server'` marks an async server-side function as callable from client-side code. A framework turns it into a server reference; calling that reference sends serializable arguments over the network and returns a serialized result.

parameters.name: function arguments
parameters.description: Arguments passed to the async Server Function; they must use types supported by React serialization.

use server.returns: A serialized function result delivered to the client; the function itself must return a Promise because it is async.

example.title: Module-level Server Function
example.explanation: The module directive makes the exported async function callable from client code through the framework's server-function mechanism.

useCases.title: Client-triggered mutations
useCases.scenario: Expose a server-side mutation such as adding an item to a cart while keeping database access on the server.

useCases.title: Shared server-function modules
useCases.scenario: Place the directive at module scope so several exported async functions can be imported by Client Components.

useCases.title: Form submissions
useCases.scenario: Use a function as a form `action` or `formAction` so React invokes it in a Transition.

interview.question: What does `'use server'` do?
interview.answer: It marks an async server-side function as callable by client code. The framework creates a reference, and invoking that reference sends a request to the server and returns the serialized result.
interview.followUp: Can a synchronous function use it? No. The documentation says the directive can only be used on async functions because the underlying call is a network operation.

interview.question: What is the difference between function-level and module-level usage?
interview.answer: A module-level directive marks every export in that file as a Server Function, allowing those exports to be imported by client code. A function-level directive marks only that function.
interview.followUp: Why is module scope needed for client imports? The documentation requires the directive at module level when Server Functions are imported from client code.

interview.question: What constraints apply when calling a Server Function?
interview.answer: Arguments cross a network boundary, so they must use React's supported serializable types. Server Functions should also be treated as public entry points: validate untrusted arguments and authorize mutations.
interview.followUp: How should UI code invoke one? Prefer a Transition; functions supplied to a form's `action` or `formAction` are automatically invoked in a Transition.

keyPoints: It exposes a server-side function through a client-callable server reference.
React's current documentation calls these callable server-side functions Server Functions.
A client invocation performs a network request rather than executing the function locally.
Return values cross back to the client through serialization.
A file-level directive applies to every exported function in that module.
Arguments must be serializable because they cross the client-server boundary.
Wrap ordinary client-triggered calls in a Transition; form actions receive this handling automatically.
gotchas: The directive belongs only in server-side files; it does not designate a Server Component.
Only async functions can use the directive because invoking them requires an asynchronous network request.
Validate and authorize every request before performing a mutation.
Place the directive first, before imports or other executable code; comments may precede it.

useActionState.summary: useActionState updates component state from a form action's result. It returns the latest state, a form-compatible action, and a pending flag.
useActionState.explanation: Call this Hook at component level with an action and initial serializable state. React passes the previous state into the action, then returns the action's latest result, a form-compatible wrapped action, and a pending flag.
useActionState.syntax: const [state, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(fn, initialState, permalink?);

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Function called when the form is submitted or a button is pressed. It receives previous form state first, then the normal form-action arguments.

parameters.name: initialState
parameters.description: Initial state value. It may be any serializable value and is used before the action runs.

parameters.name: permalink
parameters.description: Optional permalink used with progressive enhancement for forms that may submit before hydration.

useActionState.returns: An array: [state, formAction, isPending]. state is the current or latest action result; formAction is the wrapped action for a form or button; isPending indicates whether a Transition is pending.

example.title: Form action with validation and pending UI
example.explanation: The action receives the previous state and submitted FormData, while the hook exposes the latest result and pending status for the form UI.

useCases.title: Form result handling
useCases.scenario: Show validation errors or a success message returned by a submitted form action.

useCases.title: Pending-state feedback
useCases.scenario: Disable inputs and display progress while an asynchronous action is running.

useCases.title: Server-backed forms
useCases.scenario: Use a server function while preserving progressive enhancement and the latest response.

useCases.title: Manual action invocation
useCases.scenario: Invoke an action within a transition when a form element is not the direct caller.

keyPoints: Use it when a form submission should update component state from the action's returned result.
The action receives its previous state first, followed by the arguments normally supplied to a form action.
The state represents the most recent completed action result.
Use the returned action as a form action or as a button's formAction.
The returned action is not limited to declarative form submission; it can also be invoked within a transition.
Use isPending to disable controls or show progress while the action is pending.
gotchas: It is a Hook, so call it at the top level of a component or custom Hook—not inside loops or conditions.
The initialState value only seeds the first render; later state comes from the action's returned value.
Use an initial state that can be serialized, especially when integrating with server-rendered or server-function workflows.

useCallback.summary: useCallback caches a function definition between component renders. React reuses the cached function while its dependencies remain unchanged.
useCallback.explanation: At the component or custom Hook’s top level, useCallback receives a function and every reactive value that function reads. React returns the initial function first, then reuses the previous function when dependencies are unchanged and supplies the current function when they differ.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: The function definition to cache; it may accept any arguments and return any values.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: The list of reactive values referenced by fn, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component.

useCallback.returns: On the first render, the supplied function; on later renders, either the previously stored function when dependencies are unchanged or the current function when they changed.

example.title: Stable callback for a memoized child
example.explanation: The cached callback keeps the same identity while its dependencies remain unchanged, allowing the memoized button to skip unnecessary re-renders.

useCases.title: Stabilize a callback prop
useCases.scenario: A memoized child receives a callback prop and should not re-render solely because the parent rendered again.

useCases.title: Control Hook dependencies
useCases.scenario: A callback is included in another Hook’s dependency list and should change only when its reactive inputs change.

useCases.title: Avoid unnecessary resubscriptions
useCases.scenario: An external subscription API uses callback identity to determine whether it must resubscribe.

interview.question: What does useCallback do?
interview.answer: useCallback caches a function definition between renders. It returns the original function on the first render, then reuses it when the dependency list has not changed.
interview.followUp: Why can this matter for a child component? A stable callback prop can help a memoized child avoid a re-render caused only by function identity changing.

interview.question: How should dependencies be chosen?
interview.answer: The dependency list contains every reactive value referenced by the callback, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component. React compares dependencies with Object.is.
interview.followUp: What happens when one dependency changes? React returns the function created during the current render and stores it for later reuse.

interview.question: When is useCallback useful?
interview.answer: useCallback is most useful when a cached function is passed to a component wrapped in memo, or when its identity is itself used as a dependency of another Hook. It is not a general requirement for every event handler.
interview.followUp: What should be tried first when a component is slow? Profile the application and optimize the actual bottleneck rather than adding memoization indiscriminately.

keyPoints: It preserves a callback’s function identity across renders until its dependencies change.
The Hook belongs at the component or custom Hook’s top level, following the Rules of Hooks.
The dependency array should include every reactive value read by the callback.
The first render returns the exact function supplied to the Hook.
Later renders reuse the stored callback when dependencies remain equal.
React compares dependency values with Object.is to decide whether the cached function can be reused.
gotchas: Call useCallback only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; do not place it inside a loop or conditional.
The cache is an optimization rather than a semantic guarantee; code must remain correct even if React discards the cached function.

useContext.summary: useContext reads and subscribes a component to a context. It returns the nearest provider's value, or the context's defaultValue when no provider is above the component.
useContext.explanation: useContext reads a previously created context and subscribes the calling component to its value. React selects the nearest provider above that component, falls back to the context default when none exists, and re-renders consumers when the value changes.

parameters.name: SomeContext
parameters.description: The context object previously created with createContext; for example, ThemeContext.

useContext.returns: The current context value for the calling component: the value from the closest matching provider above it, or the createContext defaultValue when no provider exists.

example.title: Read a theme from context
example.explanation: Button reads the nearest theme value and updates when App changes the context.

useCases.title: Cross-cutting UI settings
useCases.scenario: Share a theme, locale, or other display preference across a component subtree without threading props through every intermediate component.

useCases.title: Shared application services
useCases.scenario: Expose application-wide services or configuration such as an API client, authentication state, or feature flags to descendants.

useCases.title: Scoped overrides
useCases.scenario: Select different values for nested sections by placing a closer provider around each section.

interview.question: How does useContext choose the value it returns?
interview.answer: useContext takes a context object created with createContext and returns the value supplied by the closest matching provider above the calling component. Without such a provider, it returns the context's default value.
interview.followUp: What happens when the provider value changes? React automatically re-renders components that read that context, and their returned value stays current.

interview.question: Where may useContext be called, and what does the subscription do?
interview.answer: Call useContext at the top level of a component. The Hook subscribes that component to the context, so React can update it when the context value changes.
interview.followUp: Can a provider created in the same component affect that component's call? No; the provider must be above the component making the call.

interview.question: What is passed to useContext, and how do nested providers work?
interview.answer: The context object is the parameter, such as useContext(ThemeContext). The context itself represents the kind of information being provided or read; its value comes from the nearest provider.
interview.followUp: How can a consumer receive a different value from a nested part of the tree? Put a closer matching provider above that consumer; it shadows outer providers.

keyPoints: It combines reading a context value with a subscription to subsequent changes.
The Hook's call returns the current value associated with the supplied context object.
Provider lookup follows the rendered tree and selects the nearest matching provider above the consumer.
A consumer does not need to manually synchronize its local copy with context.
Changing a consumed context value causes React to update the reading components.
Pass the context object returned by createContext, not an arbitrary value, to useContext.
gotchas: A provider returned by the same component does not affect that component's own useContext call; place the provider above the consumer.
Nested providers shadow outer providers for consumers beneath them.
Do not call the Hook inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
The createContext default is used only when no matching provider exists above the consumer.

useDebugValue.summary: useDebugValue lets a custom Hook expose a readable label or value in React DevTools. An optional formatter controls how the value appears when the component is inspected.
useDebugValue.explanation: Call useDebugValue inside a custom Hook to expose a value or readable label in React DevTools. React displays the value directly unless you provide a formatter; with one, DevTools invokes it when the component is inspected and displays its result.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to display in React DevTools; it can have any type.

parameters.name: format
parameters.description: Optional function that receives value and returns the formatted value displayed by React DevTools when the component is inspected.

useDebugValue.returns: Nothing; useDebugValue does not return a value.

example.title: Label a custom Hook
example.explanation: The custom Hook exposes a readable online-status label in React DevTools while returning the underlying status to its caller.

useCases.title: Show a concise status label
useCases.scenario: A custom Hook exposes a boolean or enum state

useCases.title: Present an inspection-friendly representation
useCases.scenario: A custom Hook stores complex data

useCases.title: Defer presentation formatting to DevTools
useCases.scenario: Formatting is expensive or unnecessary during normal rendering

interview.question: What problem does useDebugValue solve?
interview.answer: useDebugValue adds a custom Hook label or value to React DevTools. It returns nothing and is intended for making custom Hook state easier to inspect.
interview.followUp: How can expensive formatting be deferred? Pass a formatter as the second argument; DevTools calls it when the component is inspected rather than requiring the formatted value on every Hook call.

interview.question: What are useDebugValue's arguments?
interview.answer: The first argument is the value shown in DevTools and may have any type. If no formatter is supplied, React DevTools displays that original value.
interview.followUp: What happens if the formatter returns a non-string? The returned value is still used as the formatted display value, because the documentation allows it to have any type.

interview.question: Where should the Hook be called and what should it display?
interview.answer: Place useDebugValue at the top level of the custom Hook. A common pattern is to convert internal state into a concise status such as Online or Offline for inspection.
interview.followUp: Should every custom Hook use it? No; use it when a meaningful developer-facing label improves inspection, rather than adding noise to simple Hooks.

keyPoints: It gives custom Hooks a developer-facing label in React DevTools, making their internal state easier to recognize during inspection.
Use it at the custom Hook's top level, just like other Hooks.
Its first argument is the debug value to expose, and that value can be any type.
Without a formatter, DevTools shows the first argument directly.
A formatter receives the supplied debug value and returns what DevTools should display.
The Hook has no return value; it exists only to improve custom Hook debugging.
gotchas: Invoke it at the custom Hook's top level, following the Rules of Hooks; do not place it inside conditions or nested functions.
A formatter may run when DevTools inspects the component, so keep formatting focused on presentation and avoid side effects.

useDeferredValue.summary: useDeferredValue lets you defer updating a non-critical part of the UI so urgent updates can appear first. It returns a value that may temporarily lag behind the latest input.
useDeferredValue.explanation: Call this Hook with a value at the top level of a component. React returns the current value initially, then may render with the previous value first and retry in the background with the new value, allowing urgent UI such as typing to update before slower content.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to defer; it can have any type.

parameters.name: initialValue
parameters.description: Optional value used during the component's initial render. Without it, the initial render is not deferred.

useDeferredValue.returns: The current deferred value: initially initialValue when supplied, otherwise the provided value; during updates it may remain the old value before switching to the new value after background rendering.

example.title: Responsive search
example.explanation: The input responds immediately while filtering can continue with the deferred query.

useCases.title: Keep typing responsive
useCases.scenario: A controlled search input updates immediately while an expensive results list consumes a deferred query.

useCases.title: Show stale content during loading
useCases.scenario: A Suspense-backed result view continues using the previous query while fresh content loads.

useCases.title: Defer expensive rendering
useCases.scenario: A large derived view recalculates from a deferred primitive, allowing higher-priority interactions to proceed.

interview.question: How does useDeferredValue affect rendering?
interview.answer: It returns a deferred version of the supplied value. On updates, React can first render with the old value and then attempt a background render using the new one, keeping urgent UI responsive.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from debouncing? React does not use a fixed delay; the background render is interruptible and does not block user input.

interview.question: What is initialValue for?
interview.answer: The optional initialValue is used for the component's initial render. If omitted, the Hook does not defer that first render because no previous value exists.
interview.followUp: What happens after the initial render? React schedules work with the supplied value so the component can update in the background.

interview.question: What values should be passed to the Hook?
interview.answer: The Hook compares the incoming value with the previous one using Object.is. Values should therefore be primitives or stable objects created outside rendering.
interview.followUp: Why is an inline object problematic? A newly created object differs on every render, which can cause unnecessary background renders.

keyPoints: Use it when a non-critical UI region should update after more urgent parts, such as an input.
Invoke it at component top level and store the returned value for the slower subtree or calculation.
The consumer can temporarily display content based on the previous value while React prepares the fresh result.
React follows the initial update with background work that uses the latest value.
Supplying initialValue lets the first render use a fallback-like value before the deferred input is applied.
gotchas: Prefer primitives or objects created outside rendering; creating a new object during rendering can trigger unnecessary background work.

useFormStatus.summary: `useFormStatus` lets a component rendered inside a form read the status of its parent form submission. Use it to show pending UI, inspect submitted data, or access the form method and function action.
useFormStatus.explanation: `useFormStatus` reads submission status from the nearest parent `<form>`, allowing descendants such as reusable buttons to react without receiving status props. It returns whether submission is pending plus the submitted `FormData`, HTTP method, and function action when applicable.
useFormStatus.syntax: const { pending, data, method, action } = useFormStatus();
useFormStatus.returns: An object with `pending`, `data`, `method`, and `action`. `pending` is boolean; `data` is `FormData` or `null`; `method` is `'get'` or `'post'`; and `action` is the parent form's function action or `null`.

example.title: Disable a submit button while the form action runs
example.explanation: A submit button reads its parent form's pending state and disables itself while the action runs.

useCases.title: Pending submit feedback
useCases.scenario: Disable a submit control and change its label while the form action is running.

useCases.title: Context-free form controls
useCases.scenario: Build reusable design-system controls that react to their containing form without prop drilling.

useCases.title: Submission metadata
useCases.scenario: Inspect the submitted fields or determine whether the parent form uses GET or POST.

interview.question: What problem does `useFormStatus` solve, and where is it imported from?
interview.answer: It reads status from the parent form through the component tree, so a descendant can update its UI without receiving pending state through props. The Hook is imported from `react-dom`, not `react`.
interview.followUp: What does it observe when multiple forms exist? It observes only the nearest relevant parent form, not a form rendered by the same component or a child component.

interview.question: What does `useFormStatus` return?
interview.answer: The Hook takes no arguments and returns an object containing `pending`, `data`, `method`, and `action`. `pending` is true while the parent form is submitting.
interview.followUp: What are the inactive values? `data` is null without an active submission or parent form, and `action` is null without a parent form or function action.

interview.question: How would you use it to provide submission feedback?
interview.answer: Place the Hook in a component rendered inside the form, commonly a submit button. Use `pending` to disable the button or show a submitting label while the form action runs.
interview.followUp: Can the Hook be placed in the form-rendering component before its `<form>` output? No; it must execute in a component rendered inside the form.

keyPoints: Use it when a descendant needs access to the parent form's latest submission status.
Call it with empty parentheses; configuration comes from the surrounding parent form.
The `pending` boolean indicates that the parent form is actively submitting.
During an active submission, `data` exposes the submitted fields as `FormData`.
The `method` field reports whether the parent form submits with GET or POST.
When the form has a function action, `action` identifies that function.
gotchas: Call the Hook in a descendant component, not directly in the component that renders the `<form>`.
The status belongs to the parent form; a nested or separately rendered form is not observed by the component that owns it.
The action field is only populated when the parent form uses a function action.

useId.summary: useId generates unique strings for connecting elements through accessibility attributes. Call it at the top level of a component or custom Hook, with no arguments.
useId.explanation: Call useId at the top level of a component or custom Hook to obtain a stable unique string for the mounted component. Pass that string to related accessibility attributes, such as aria-describedby, so elements can reference one another without manually coordinating IDs.
useId.returns: A unique ID string associated with the particular useId call in the component.

example.title: Associate an input with its hint
example.explanation: Generates a component-specific ID and connects the input to its accessibility hint.

useCases.title: Accessible form descriptions
useCases.scenario: A form control needs to reference helper or validation text through aria-describedby.

useCases.title: Reusable component relationships
useCases.scenario: Several component instances need internally coordinated IDs without manually passing them from a parent.

useCases.title: SSR-compatible accessibility IDs
useCases.scenario: Server-rendered markup must preserve matching control-to-description references across hydration.

interview.question: What does useId return, and what is its main purpose?
interview.answer: useId generates a unique ID string associated with a particular useId call in a component. The intended use is connecting elements through accessibility attributes.
interview.followUp: Why not use it for list keys? Keys should come from the underlying data, while useId is intended for IDs in the rendered accessibility relationship.

interview.question: Where can useId be called?
interview.answer: No parameters are required. Call it at the component or custom Hook's top level, not inside a loop or condition.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a variable number of repeated fields? Extract each repeated field into a component so each instance can call the Hook at its own top level.

interview.question: What constraint does useId have with server rendering?
interview.answer: With server rendering, the server and client must render an identical component tree. If their trees differ, the generated IDs will not match.
interview.followUp: What is the practical implication for hydration? Keep conditional rendering and component structure consistent between server and client, especially around components using useId.

keyPoints: Use it to create IDs for relationships between accessible elements, such as a control and its descriptive text.
The Hook has no configuration arguments; invoke it directly.
Each call produces a string tied to that call site and component instance.
Treat the generated value as a rendering identifier, not as a permanent external identifier.
Reuse the value across attributes that need to reference the same element.
gotchas: Call it only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; move conditional or repeated state into a separate component.
Do not use this Hook in an async Server Component.
Server-rendered and client-rendered trees must match for generated IDs to stay aligned.

useImperativeHandle.summary: useImperativeHandle customizes the value exposed through a ref. In React 19, a component can receive ref as a prop and expose a restricted object of imperative methods instead of its underlying DOM node.
useImperativeHandle.explanation: Call this Hook at the top level of a component to replace the usual ref value with a custom handle. The handle factory returns any value, commonly an object of methods. Include every reactive value used by that factory in the dependency list so React can recreate the handle when those values change; in React 19, a function component receives ref as a prop.

parameters.name: ref
parameters.description: The ref received by the component; this is the ref whose exposed value will be customized.

parameters.name: createHandle
parameters.description: A zero-argument function that returns the value to expose through the ref.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline, constant-length list of all reactive values used by createHandle.

example.title: Expose a restricted input API
example.explanation: The child keeps its DOM ref private while exposing only focus and clear methods to the parent.

useCases.title: Expose selected input actions
useCases.scenario: A parent needs to focus, select, scroll, or clear a child-controlled input without owning its DOM node.

useCases.title: Hide implementation details
useCases.scenario: A component wraps a complex widget but should reveal only a small command API.

useCases.title: Bridge imperative APIs
useCases.scenario: A child must provide an imperative operation that cannot be expressed naturally with declarative props.

useCases.title: Publish reactive methods
useCases.scenario: A ref handle depends on current props or state and must be refreshed when those values change.

interview.question: What problem does useImperativeHandle solve?
interview.answer: It customizes the value exposed through a ref. The factory returns the handle, which can be any type and is often an object containing a small set of methods.
interview.followUp: Why use it instead of exposing a DOM node? A custom handle limits the parent to intentional operations and keeps the DOM implementation private.

interview.question: How should dependencies be specified?
interview.answer: The dependency list contains every reactive value read by the factory, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component. React compares dependencies with Object.is and recreates the handle when one changes or when no list is supplied.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to the list? It must have a constant number of entries and be written inline.

interview.question: How is ref received in React 19?
interview.answer: In React 19, ref is available as a prop, so a function component can pass that prop directly to useImperativeHandle. The Hook returns undefined and must be called at the component’s top level.
interview.followUp: How would this differ in older React code? Components commonly used forwardRef to receive the ref, but React 19 documents ref as a prop.

keyPoints: It replaces the default ref exposure with a deliberately chosen handle.
Call it unconditionally at the component’s top level, not inside branches or loops.
The factory accepts no arguments and returns the complete exposed value.
The exposed handle is not restricted to an object; it may use any value type.
A compact methods object is the usual way to provide a narrow imperative API.
Dependency changes are detected with Object.is semantics.
gotchas: Keep the dependency array inline and fixed-length; it is not a dynamically sized list.
Do not omit reactive props, state, or component-local variables referenced by the factory.

useInsertionEffect.summary: useInsertionEffect lets CSS-in-JS libraries insert styles before layout effects run. It is a specialized client-side hook, not a general replacement for useEffect or useLayoutEffect.
useInsertionEffect.explanation: useInsertionEffect runs an effect setup when a component is added, before layout effects run, and repeats cleanup followed by setup when dependencies change. It is intended for CSS-in-JS libraries that must inject styles early; its cleanup runs when the component is removed.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Effect logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional list of every reactive value referenced by setup, including props, state, and component-body declarations.

example.title: Inject a CSS rule
example.explanation: This component adds a CSS rule before layout effects and removes the corresponding style element during cleanup.

useCases.title: Inject generated styles
useCases.scenario: A CSS-in-JS library creates or updates a style element when generated rules change.

useCases.title: Clean up injected rules
useCases.scenario: A styling library removes a previously inserted rule when its owning component unmounts or its rule changes.

interview.question: What problem does useInsertionEffect solve?
interview.answer: It is a specialized effect for CSS-in-JS libraries. React runs its setup before layout effects, allowing styles to be inserted before effects that may measure layout.
interview.followUp: Why should ordinary components usually avoid it? Use useEffect or useLayoutEffect instead unless the code is implementing a CSS-in-JS library that needs this insertion point.

interview.question: Describe its cleanup lifecycle.
interview.answer: The setup function may return cleanup. On dependency changes, React runs cleanup with the old values and then setup with the new values; on unmount, it runs cleanup.
interview.followUp: What must the dependency list contain? Every reactive value referenced by setup, including props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component body.

interview.question: What constraints apply while the hook runs?
interview.answer: It returns undefined and runs only on the client. It cannot update state, refs are not attached yet, and DOM update timing should not be assumed.
interview.followUp: How should server-rendered CSS be handled? The documentation only establishes that this effect does not run during server rendering, so CSS-in-JS code must not depend on this hook for server output.

keyPoints: Reserve this hook for CSS-in-JS library implementation rather than normal application logic.
For most application code, choose useEffect or useLayoutEffect instead.
Use it to place style insertion ahead of layout-sensitive effects.
Initial setup occurs after mounting and before layout effects.
Changed dependencies cause cleanup with old values before new setup runs.
Unmounting invokes the cleanup returned by setup.
gotchas: Do not update state from this hook.
Refs are unavailable when the hook executes.
Do not assume that the DOM has already been updated.
The hook does not run during server rendering.

useLayoutEffect.summary: useLayoutEffect runs before the browser repaints, making it suitable for layout reads and visual corrections that must not flicker. Prefer useEffect unless the work must happen before paint.
useLayoutEffect.explanation: useLayoutEffect runs after React commits DOM changes but before the browser repaints. Use it when a visual effect must synchronously read layout and possibly update state before the user sees the result; otherwise prefer useEffect.

parameters.name: setup
parameters.description: Function containing the effect logic; it may optionally return a cleanup function.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: Optional inline list of reactive values referenced by setup.

example.title: Measure a tooltip before paint
example.explanation: Measures the tooltip before the browser paints, allowing its position to use the measured height without a visible intermediate layout.

useCases.title: Measure and position visual elements
useCases.scenario: A tooltip or popover needs its DOM dimensions to calculate a position before becoming visible.

useCases.title: Synchronize rendering with DOM geometry
useCases.scenario: A component must read an element's bounding box immediately after commit and use it to render a corrected layout.

useCases.title: Coordinate layout-sensitive integrations
useCases.scenario: An external visual system requires setup and teardown that must occur before repaint.

interview.question: What distinguishes useLayoutEffect from useEffect?
interview.answer: useLayoutEffect is the layout-sensitive counterpart to useEffect. It runs before the browser repaints, so it can measure DOM layout and update state before the user sees the result.
interview.followUp: When should useEffect be preferred? Prefer it for ordinary side effects, because useLayoutEffect blocks painting and can make the app slower.

interview.question: How do setup and dependencies control this Hook?
interview.answer: The setup function contains the effect logic and may return cleanup logic. The optional dependency list contains reactive values referenced by setup; React reruns the effect when those dependencies change.
interview.followUp: What should the dependency list look like? It should have a constant number of items and be written inline, such as [dep1, dep2].

interview.question: What server-rendering limitation applies?
interview.answer: Effects run only on the client, not during server rendering. Therefore, layout measurements must happen after the component is available in the browser.
interview.followUp: What alternative avoids blocking the initial paint? Replace useLayoutEffect with useEffect when an initial visual adjustment does not need to happen before paint.

keyPoints: Use it for visual work that must finish before paint, such as measuring or positioning an element.
A common pattern is to read an element's geometry, store the result in state, and render using that measurement.
Return cleanup code when the effect subscribes, attaches listeners, or otherwise needs to undo external work.
Include every reactive value used by setup in the dependency list so the measurement or synchronization stays current.
Use the Hook for its side effects; it does not produce a value for the component to consume.
gotchas: Call the Hook only at the top level of a component or custom Hook; move conditional behavior into the effect or extract a component.
Do not depend on this Hook for server-rendered measurements or other server-side effects.
Because its code and state updates block repainting, reserve it for effects that genuinely need to run before paint.

useMemo.summary: useMemo caches the result of a calculation between component renders. React reuses that result while its dependencies remain unchanged and recalculates it when they change.
useMemo.explanation: Call useMemo at the top level with a pure, argument-free calculation and an inline dependency list. React returns the cached result when every dependency is unchanged by Object.is; otherwise it runs the calculation again and stores the new result.

parameters.name: calculateValue
parameters.description: A pure, argument-free function that computes the value to cache; React calls it during the initial render and when dependencies change.

parameters.name: dependencies
parameters.description: An inline list containing every reactive value used by calculateValue; it must contain a constant number of items.

useMemo.returns: The cached calculation result, or a newly computed result when dependencies change.

example.title: Cache a derived list
example.explanation: The filtered array is reused when neither todos nor tab changes.

useCases.title: Skip expensive recalculations
useCases.scenario: A component repeatedly renders while an expensive derived value has unchanged inputs.

useCases.title: Preserve stable references
useCases.scenario: A memoized child needs a stable derived object or array so unchanged props can remain referentially equal.

useCases.title: Cache client-component computations
useCases.scenario: A client component needs to retain an expensive computation across its renders.

interview.question: What does useMemo do?
interview.answer: useMemo caches a calculation result between renders. React compares the dependency entries with their previous values using Object.is; unchanged dependencies reuse the prior value, while changed dependencies trigger recalculation.
interview.followUp: What must the calculation and dependency list look like? The calculation should be pure and take no arguments, and the list should include every reactive value it reads with a constant inline shape.

interview.question: Where may useMemo be called?
interview.answer: Call it at the top level of a component or custom Hook, never inside a loop or condition. Its purpose is to cache a computed value, not to perform side effects.
interview.followUp: How should conditional computation be structured? Extract a component or custom Hook so the Hook call remains unconditional at the top level.

interview.question: How do you choose dependencies?
interview.answer: The dependency list must contain every value from the component used by the calculation, including props, state, and locally declared variables or functions. React uses that list to decide whether the cached value remains valid.
interview.followUp: What happens when a dependency is omitted? React may reuse a stale result because the change is invisible to the dependency comparison.

keyPoints: It memoizes a computed value so later renders can reuse it.
The calculation receives no arguments, has no side effects, and returns the value to cache.
When every dependency is Object.is-equal to its previous value, React returns the existing cached value.
Any changed dependency invalidates the cache and causes the calculation to execute again.
Dependencies should cover all reactive values referenced by the calculation.
gotchas: Do not call useMemo inside loops or conditions; move conditional logic into a separate component or Hook.
Keep the dependency array inline with a fixed number of entries; include every reactive value used by the calculation.

useOptimistic.summary: useOptimistic lets a component display temporary optimistic state while an Action is pending. After the Action finishes or errors, React returns to the source value.
useOptimistic.explanation: useOptimistic creates temporary UI state for an in-progress Action. React displays the optimistic value during the Action, then uses the source value again after the Action finishes or fails.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value used when no Action is pending and after the optimistic Action is complete.

parameters.name: reducer
parameters.description: Optional pure function receiving the current optimistic state and an action, returning the next optimistic state.

useOptimistic.returns: An array containing optimisticState and set. optimisticState is the value or reducer-derived temporary state; set updates it inside an Action.

example.title: Optimistic like count
example.explanation: The count changes immediately during the Action and returns to the source value when the Action completes.

useCases.title: Instant mutation feedback
useCases.scenario: A user submits a form or mutation and the UI should reflect the expected result immediately.

useCases.title: Responsive controls
useCases.scenario: A network-backed control needs a temporary count, label, or status while its request is pending.

useCases.title: Optimistic list updates
useCases.scenario: A list item should appear or change immediately while the server operation completes.

interview.question: What does useOptimistic return?
interview.answer: useOptimistic returns exactly two values: the current optimistic state and a setter. Without a pending Action, the state equals the value argument; during an Action, it reflects the reducer result or the setter value.
interview.followUp: How should a reducer be designed? Keep it pure, accept the current state and action, and return the next optimistic state without side effects.

interview.question: What are the arguments to useOptimistic?
interview.answer: The first argument is the fallback value shown when no Action is pending. The optional reducer describes how an optimistic update transforms current state in response to an action.
interview.followUp: What happens after the Action completes? React goes back to rendering the value supplied as the first argument.

interview.question: How do you apply an optimistic update safely?
interview.answer: The setter must run inside an Action, commonly inside startTransition. React then re-renders with the optimistic value while the asynchronous work is pending.
interview.followUp: What if the setter runs outside an Action? React warns, and the optimistic state only renders briefly before the source value is used again.

keyPoints: Use it when the interface should show an expected result before background work finishes.
The Hook returns a state value and a function for requesting an optimistic value.
The first argument is the authoritative value displayed when no Action is pending.
The first returned item is the state currently rendered by the component.
The second returned item schedules the temporary state used during an Action.
Calling the setter in an Action immediately re-renders the UI with the requested optimistic state.
gotchas: Call the setter within an Action, such as the callback passed to startTransition; otherwise React warns and the optimistic rendering is only temporary.
A reducer must be pure and derive the next optimistic state only from its arguments.
Like other Hooks, call useOptimistic at component top level rather than inside conditions or loops.

useSyncExternalStore.summary: useSyncExternalStore lets a component read from and subscribe to an external store. It supports server rendering through an optional server snapshot and re-renders when the snapshot changes.
useSyncExternalStore.explanation: Call this Hook at the component’s top level with a subscription function and a snapshot reader. React invokes the reader after store notifications, compares snapshots, and re-renders when the value changes; an optional third function supplies the server and hydration snapshot.

parameters.name: subscribe
parameters.description: Subscribes to the store with a callback and returns a cleanup function that unsubscribes.

parameters.name: getSnapshot
parameters.description: Returns the immutable snapshot needed by the component; unchanged store state must produce the same value.

parameters.name: getServerSnapshot
parameters.description: Optional initial snapshot used during server rendering and hydration; it must match between server and client.

useSyncExternalStore.returns: The current snapshot of the external store.

example.title: Subscribe to browser online status
example.explanation: Reads browser connectivity through a stable subscription and supplies a server fallback for hydration.

useCases.title: External state libraries
useCases.scenario: A state-management library exposes data outside React and needs concurrent-safe React integration.

useCases.title: Browser subscriptions
useCases.scenario: A browser API such as online/offline status changes independently of React state.

useCases.title: SSR and hydration
useCases.scenario: A server-rendered component reads external data that must match during hydration.

interview.question: How does useSyncExternalStore detect external-store changes?
interview.answer: The Hook connects React to a store outside React. subscribe registers a callback and returns cleanup, while getSnapshot reads the data; React calls getSnapshot after notifications and re-renders when its result changes by Object.is.
interview.followUp: Why must snapshots be cached? Repeated reads must return the same value when the store is unchanged, so a new object on every read can trigger endless updates.

interview.question: What contract does subscribe implement?
interview.answer: subscribe receives React’s callback and must invoke it whenever the store changes. It must also return a cleanup function that removes the subscription.
interview.followUp: What if subscribe changes identity between renders? React resubscribes using the new function, so define stable subscription logic when possible.

interview.question: When is getServerSnapshot required?
interview.answer: getServerSnapshot supplies the initial store value during server rendering and client hydration. The server and client values must match, commonly by serializing the server value for the client.
interview.followUp: What happens without it in SSR? Rendering the component on the server throws an error.

keyPoints: Use it to read data managed outside React while letting React coordinate subscription updates.
Invoke the Hook at component top level, not inside conditions, loops, or nested functions.
Implement subscribe as a registration operation whose returned cleanup reverses that registration.
Provide a reader for the portion of external-store state required by the component.
The store must notify React through the callback whenever its relevant data changes.
React uses Object.is semantics on snapshot results to decide whether the component needs another render.
gotchas: Return immutable snapshots. For mutable underlying data, create a new immutable snapshot only when the store changes; otherwise reuse the cached snapshot.
Cache the snapshot while the store is unchanged; unstable results can cause unnecessary work or an infinite update loop.
When server rendering, provide a third argument whose result matches the client’s initial snapshot during hydration.
Server-rendered components need getServerSnapshot; omitting it causes server rendering to fail.

useTransition.summary: useTransition lets a component mark non-urgent state updates as background Transitions. It returns a pending flag and a function for starting them.
useTransition.explanation: Call this Hook at component level to obtain a pending indicator and a function for marking state updates as Transitions. The callback runs immediately; synchronous updates inside it receive transition priority, while async work in React 19 can keep the pending state active and requires wrapping post-await state updates in another transition.
useTransition.returns: An array containing [isPending, startTransition]. isPending is a boolean indicating whether a Transition is pending; startTransition is a function that marks updates in its callback as Transitions.

example.title: Pending tab transition
example.explanation: Marks tab navigation as non-urgent and displays feedback while its transition is pending.

useCases.title: Non-blocking navigation
useCases.scenario: Keep tab, route, or panel navigation responsive while rendering the newly selected view.

useCases.title: Pending feedback
useCases.scenario: Show a spinner or disabled state while a Transition is still in progress.

useCases.title: Async updates
useCases.scenario: Run React 19 async Actions that coordinate requests and pending UI.

interview.question: What does useTransition return?
interview.answer: useTransition returns exactly two values: isPending and startTransition. The flag indicates whether a Transition is pending, and the function marks updates performed by its callback as Transitions.
interview.followUp: What should code outside a component use? Use the standalone startTransition function, but it does not provide an isPending indicator.

interview.question: Where and how is useTransition called?
interview.answer: Call useTransition at the top level of a component or custom Hook. It takes no parameters and returns the pending flag plus the transition-starting function.
interview.followUp: Why not call it conditionally? Hooks must follow React's top-level calling rules, so conditional calls would break Hook ordering.

interview.question: How does useTransition handle asynchronous Actions?
interview.answer: In React 19, startTransition can receive an async function. React sets isPending while the async transition is active; state updates after an await must be wrapped in another startTransition.
interview.followUp: What happens to urgent interaction updates? They can interrupt non-urgent transition work, keeping interactions responsive.

keyPoints: It lets React render selected UI work in the background rather than treating it as urgent.
Invoke it at component top level to obtain transition controls.
The Hook has no input arguments.
Its result is a two-item array containing the pending flag and transition function.
Use isPending to show feedback while transition work remains pending.
Wrap non-urgent state updates with startTransition.
The callback executes immediately, and synchronous state updates during it are marked as transition work.
gotchas: State updates after an async request need another startTransition wrapper.
Do not call the Hook outside a component or custom Hook; use standalone startTransition elsewhere.
The state update must occur during the callback, not later in a timer or unrelated callback.

ViewTransition.summary: `<ViewTransition>` opts a component subtree into browser View Transition animations during React Transitions and Suspense updates. It is currently available only in React’s Canary and Experimental channels.
ViewTransition.explanation: ViewTransition marks a component subtree for browser View Transition animations. React associates the nearest nested DOM node with a transition name, starts the browser transition during supported Transition or Suspense updates, and applies the default cross-fade or configured enter, exit, update, or shared-element classes.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Optional unique name for the view transition; intended for shared-element transitions.

parameters.name: enter
parameters.description: CSS class or class callback used when the component enters.

parameters.name: exit
parameters.description: CSS class or class callback used when the component exits.

parameters.name: update
parameters.description: CSS class or class callback used when the component updates.

parameters.name: share
parameters.description: CSS class or class callback used for shared-element transitions.

ViewTransition.returns: A React component that renders its children and activates browser View Transition animations for eligible updates.

example.title: Animate a Transition update

keyPoints: Wrap a subtree to opt it into React-managed View Transition animations.
The nearest nested DOM element becomes the transition's visual target.
Without custom styling, the browser supplies a cross-fade animation.
Use name when you intentionally connect matching elements across a shared-element transition.
Activation props can select CSS classes for customizing transition animations.
Transition types allow styling based on the cause of a transition.
gotchas: A direct state update does not activate the component; use a Transition, Suspense, or useDeferredValue update.
Do not provide name for ordinary animations; React generates unique names to avoid collisions.
Do not call the browser startViewTransition API manually for this feature.
